Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that all three matter, but they're not independent of each other, and compute has been the dominant driver over the past decade or so.

If you look at the trends, the amount of compute used to train frontier models has been growing at roughly four to five times per year since around 2010, when deep learning really took off. That's an enormous rate of growth, much faster than Moore's law alone would give you, because on top of hardware getting cheaper, people have been willing to spend vastly more money on training runs.

On the algorithmic side, we've done work at Epoch trying to quantify how much algorithmic progress contributes. One way to measure it is to ask: how much less compute do you need today to reach the same level of performance you could reach a few years ago? For language models, our estimates suggest the compute needed to hit a given performance level has been halving roughly every eight months or so. That's very fast, faster than Moore's law. But when you put it side by side with the scale-up in physical compute, the scale-up still accounts for the larger share of overall progress. A rough breakdown might be something like two-thirds from compute scaling and one-third from algorithmic improvements, though there's a lot of uncertainty there.

I'd also add that these aren't cleanly separable. Many algorithmic innovations, like the transformer, are valuable precisely because they scale well with more compute. Some techniques give you large gains at large scale and little at small scale, so the value of algorithmic progress depends on how much compute you have. And a lot of algorithmic research is itself compute-intensive. You need experiments to find out what works, so more compute speeds up the discovery of better algorithms.

Data is the third piece. Under the scaling laws we've seen, like the Chinchilla results, if you want to use compute efficiently you need to scale data alongside model size. So far, data hasn't been the binding constraint, because the internet has supplied huge amounts of text. But we've looked at this, and on current trends we may exhaust the stock of high-quality public human-generated text sometime in the next several years. So data could become much more important as a bottleneck, and things like synthetic data, multimodal data, or better data efficiency may become central to whether progress continues at the same pace.

So in summary: compute has been the main engine, algorithms are a substantial and complementary contributor, and data has mostly come along for the ride until now but may increasingly constrain things going forward.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So this is actually the question I've spent a lot of my time at Epoch trying to get a handle on, and I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what timescale and what domain you're looking at, but there are some things we can say fairly confidently.

If you look at the big picture over the last decade or so, the most striking thing is just how much compute has grown. Training compute for frontier models has been increasing by roughly four to five times per year, which is enormously faster than Moore's law. That growth has come from two things: hardware getting cheaper per unit of computation, and labs simply spending vastly more money. And a lot of the headline capability gains we've seen, from GPT-2 to GPT-4 and beyond, are pretty directly attributable to that scaling.

But that's not the whole story. When we've tried to decompose progress, for instance in language modeling or in computer vision, we find that algorithmic improvements have been contributing something comparable in magnitude. Our estimates suggest that the compute needed to reach a given level of performance has been halving roughly every eight months or so in language models. That's a very fast rate of algorithmic progress, and it means that in effect, algorithms are "worth" a substantial fraction of the total improvement, maybe on the order of half, though there's a lot of uncertainty in those numbers.

The way I think about it conceptually is that compute and algorithms are somewhat substitutable. An algorithmic innovation like the transformer, or better data curation, or mixture-of-experts, is essentially a multiplier on your effective compute. So you can think of progress as effective compute growing at the product of physical compute growth and algorithmic efficiency growth. And both of those have been moving fast.

Data is interesting because it's been less of a binding constraint historically, in the sense that labs could mostly scrape more text from the internet as they needed it. But our projections suggest that for high-quality text data in particular, we may run into limits within the next several years if current trends continue. So data could shift from being relatively abundant to being something that labs have to actively work around, through synthetic data, through multimodal data, through getting more out of each token with better training methods. In that sense, I'd say data is becoming more important as a constraint, even if it hasn't been the main driver of progress so far.

One more point I'd make is that these factors aren't independent. A lot of what looks like algorithmic progress is enabled by having more compute to run experiments. And the willingness to invest in compute is driven by the fact that scaling has been working. So there's a feedback loop where all three are pushing on each other, and trying to attribute credit too cleanly can be a bit misleading. But if you forced me to give a rough split for the recent period, I'd say compute scaling and algorithmic progress have been roughly comparable in their contribution, with data mostly being an enabler that's going to become a more active constraint going forward.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between what you need to build an AI system and what drives improvements over time. Compute, algorithms, and data are complementary inputs, so attributing progress to any one of them is tricky. Better algorithms can let you make more effective use of compute, and more compute can let you train on more data.

One way to make the comparison is to ask how much additional compute you would need to achieve the same performance without an algorithmic improvement. That gives you a common unit for comparing algorithmic progress with increases in compute. But the answer will depend on the task, the period you’re looking at, and what level of performance you’re targeting.

Data is particularly difficult to capture with a single number. It’s not just the quantity that matters; it’s also quality, diversity, and relevance to the task. And improvements in how you select or use data can also count as algorithmic improvements, so those categories overlap.

So I wouldn’t assign a fixed percentage to each. Compute is relatively straightforward to measure, which makes its contribution more visible. But that shouldn’t lead us to conclude that algorithms or data are secondary. The important question is how improvements in these inputs interact, and which one becomes the constraint as you scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between what drives progress when we scale up an existing approach and what drives progress over time. For a given approach, compute and data are complementary: more computation lets you train a larger model or train it for longer, but you generally need enough useful data to take advantage of that. Algorithms determine how efficiently you can turn those resources into capabilities.

One way to compare them is to ask how much additional compute you would need to achieve the same performance without an algorithmic improvement. That gives you a notion of algorithmic progress measured in compute equivalents. An improvement that halves the compute needed for a particular level of performance can, in that sense, have an effect similar to doubling your compute budget.

But it’s difficult to assign each factor a clean share of progress, because they interact. More compute enables researchers to try new algorithms, and better algorithms can make it worthwhile to train on much more data. Data quality also matters, so simply counting tokens doesn’t capture its contribution.

My overall view is that compute scaling has been a major driver, but treating it as the whole story would substantially understate the importance of algorithmic progress. And the relative contribution of data is particularly hard to measure independently of those other two factors.
